We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts list: 168.30, 130.70, 130.27, 128.35, 126.66, 124.85, 123.57, 58.70, 36.40, 36.40, 26.40.

We need number of methyl (CH3) groups in the molecule. Methyl carbon typically appears around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but can be around 20-30 for typical. In this list, we have 26.40 (likely methyl). Also 36.40 appears twice (maybe methylene or tertiary carbon). 58.70 maybe carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3). 168.30 carbonyl. Aromatic carbons around 120-130.

Thus likely only one methyl carbon at 26.40. However O-CH3 (methoxy) appears around 55-60 ppm, which could be a methyl attached to O. That is also a methyl group (CH3). So there could be two methyl groups: one aliphatic (26.4) and one methoxy (58.7). The question: "How many methyl (CH3) groups are present in the sample's molecule?" Methyl includes any CH3 carbon, regardless of environment. So we have two.

But need to be sure: 36.40 could be a carbon attached to two hydrogens (CH2) or a quaternary carbon? 36 ppm typical for CH2 or CH. But methyl rarely at 36. So likely not.

Thus answer 2.

We could verify with proton NMR to see number of methyl signals. Let's get proton NMR.
